title: What should a business of 40-150 staff expect from AI consulting?
description: What AI consulting should leave a firm of 40 to 150 staff with: one owner, a use rule and a measured pilot. Plus what AI seats cost at your size.
verdict: Firms of 40 to 150 staff need one owner, one use rule and one measured pilot, not a platform.[^1][^2]
Your staff likely use AI already; only about a third of owners have a written AI policy.[^3][^4]
Good help makes your people better at the work; most firms using AI report no change in headcount.[^5][^6]
Most stalled AI pilots fail on people and process, so judge any advisor on who owns the work.[^7][^8]
Free public advisors are a fair first step; hire help when you need a pilot built, measured and handed over.[^9][^10]
summary: At a firm of 40 to 150 staff with no data team, AI consulting picks one or two jobs.[^5][^11] AI drafts and sorts the work; your people check it and make the calls.[^12][^2] Staff often use AI already, so a use rule and an owner with time decide success.[^3][^1]

answers.walk-away: You should leave with a one-page AI use rule, one named owner with set hours, and one pilot with a before-and-after number.[^3][^1][^11]
answers.human-role: Your people check every AI draft and make the calls, with the owner-CEO setting the use rule and signing off anything customer-facing.[^12][^2]
answers.recipes: The work scales with firm size: one writing job at about 40 staff, one handoff fix at about 75, and one department pilot at about 150.[^12][^25][^1]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Most stalled AI pilots fail on people and process: a fuzzy problem, an owner with no time, or a build bought before the basics.[^8][^1][^31]
answers.benchmark: Judge any AI advisor by whether they name one job, one number that proves it worked, and who on your staff owns it after they leave.[^14][^1]
answers.something-else: Skip paid help under about 40 staff, or before you can pay: a free SBDC advisor or your state's MEP center is a fair first step.[^9][^10]
answers.own-data: A seat for everyone costs about $6,700 to $10,100 a year at 40 staff, $12,600 to $18,900 at 75, and $25,200 to $37,800 at 150.[^23][^24][^27][^26]

walkAway: A one-page use rule: which tools, what data may go in, and who checks the output. Only 36% of small and mid-market owners have a written AI policy.[^3][^13]
One named owner on your staff, with hours set aside each week. NIST's manufacturing program puts it plainly: "It can't be this person's third job."[^1][^2]
One pilot with a before-and-after number, such as hours or errors per job. The SBA and New York's Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) center both advise starting small.[^11][^14]
A short list of what not to use AI for. On tasks outside AI's reach, consultants using it were 19 points less likely to be right.[^15][^16]
Trained staff, not just bought seats. At firms of 50+ staff, 43% of workers got no formal AI training, says security vendor Huntress.[^17]
humanRole: Owner-CEO: sets the use rule and signs off any AI that talks to customers or touches hiring. NIST's AI framework puts AI risk decisions on executive leadership.[^2][^18]
Ops lead or GM: runs the pilot day to day, picks the job, tracks the number and can stop it. At a 200-person chemical maker, the process engineer led the AI test.[^1][^19]
Controller: checks any AI output that feeds a price, invoice or forecast. Only 25% of owners have steps to verify AI output before decisions.[^3][^12]
HR lead: owns any AI used in hiring, reviews or discipline. Colorado's law covers AI in job decisions from 1 Jan 2027, with notice and human review.[^20][^21]

recipes.name: 1. About 40 staff: a use rule, then one writing job
recipes.when: Pick this when the owner still makes most calls and staff use free AI tools. Writing tasks are where small firms use AI most (83% of users).[^12][^22]
flow: Owner-CEO: write a one-page use rule: tools, what data goes in, who checks
Ops lead: pick one writing-heavy job, like quotes or customer replies, and time it for two weeks
Ops lead: buy business seats for the pilot team only
Person sending each draft: check every AI draft before it goes out
Controller: spot-check any draft with a price or number in it
Owner-CEO: after six to eight weeks, keep it, change it or stop
recipes.cost: Ten Standard seats on ChatGPT Business or Claude Team cost $2,400 a year at list price.[^23][^24] The bigger cost is staff time for the baseline, checks and training.

recipes.name: 2. About 75 staff: find the hidden AI use, then fix one handoff
recipes.when: Pick this when staff likely use personal AI accounts. In write-ups of Census data, about 18% of firms with 50 to 99 staff don't know if staff use AI.[^25][^4]
flow: Ops lead: run a short anonymous survey of who uses which AI tool, and for what
Owner-CEO: approve one company tool and move people onto it
Ops lead: pick one slow handoff, like intake to scheduling or order to invoice
Controller: set the before-and-after number, such as days or errors per order
Team leads: train their people on the approved tool and the use rule
Owner-CEO: at eight weeks, keep it, change it or stop
recipes.cost: One business plan for 75 people runs about $12,600 to $18,900 a year at list price.[^26][^23][^27] Linking two systems adds build work, so scope and price it separately.

recipes.name: 3. About 150 staff: one department pilot, with a go-or-stop check before rollout
recipes.when: Pick this when one department head can own the work, with real time set aside. NIST's manufacturing program advises piloting one site or line before scaling.[^1][^14]
flow: Owner-CEO: name one department head as owner, with hours set aside
Department head: plan most effort on people and process, not the AI itself
HR lead: check whether anything touches hiring, reviews or discipline
Department head: run the pilot in one team or site and measure it
Owner-CEO: roll out only with a measured gain, a written check step and trained users
recipes.cost: Claude Team stops at 150 seats; Microsoft and Google business plans stop at 300 users.[^24][^27][^26] Price is driven by seats, staff time and any systems you connect.

ownData.title: What does one AI seat per person cost a 40, 75 or 150-person firm?
ownData.intro: We read four vendors' own price pages on 26 Nov 2026 and multiplied each list price by 40, 75 and 150 seats.[^23][^24][^27][^26] A seat for everyone costs about $6,700 to $37,800 a year, but a pilot needs far fewer. A ten-person pilot team costs about $1,700 to $2,500 a year.
headers: List price per seat a month
rows: Claude Team, Standard seat (2 to 150 seats)
$21, added to a Microsoft 365 plan you already pay for; $18 first-year offer to 31 Dec 2026[^27]
Google Workspace Business Standard (up to 300 users)
$14 for the whole suite with Gemini, not an AI-only add-on[^26]
ownData.note: Method: US list prices before tax, read with a web fetch tool on 26 Nov 2026. The OpenAI and Microsoft pages came from caches dated 16 and 13 Nov. Promos are left out, and the full-firm columns are a ceiling, not advice; seat price leaves out staff time, training, usage extras and build work.

watchOuts: Pilots stall when the problem is fuzzy; RAND found a misunderstood problem is the most common root cause.[^8] Name one job and one number first: 42% of firms dropped most AI projects in 2025.[^28][^29]
Staff paste company data into personal AI accounts; security vendor LayerX says 82% of pastes come from unmanaged accounts.[^30] Approve one business tool and write what data may go in.[^3]
AI gets things wrong: accuracy is the top problem small-firm AI users report (46%).[^12] Your firm owns what its chatbot tells customers, so a person checks anything customer-facing.[^18]
An owner with no time stalls the work; NIST's manufacturing program warns it "can't be this person's third job".[^1] Owner-CEO: block real hours on the ops lead's calendar before kickoff.

AI in hiring or reviews faces new state rules; Colorado's law covers job decisions from 1 Jan 2027.[^20] As of Nov 2026, a federal court order pauses enforcement, so have your HR lead check first.[^21]
Buying a build before the basics wastes money. Gartner expects firms to drop 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data, so check your data on one job first.[^31]
howToTest: Record today's numbers for one job for two weeks: volume, hours, errors and turnaround.[^11][^14]
Ask which one job they would start with, and what number proves it worked.[^14] Walk away from a plan with no named job.
Ask what they would not use AI for here. A good advisor rules some jobs out.[^16][^15]
Ask who on your staff owns it after they leave, and for how many hours a week.[^1][^2]
Ask whether it can run on tools you already pay for, like Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace.[^27][^26]
Ask to see the use rule they would write, and who signs it. NIST lists acceptable-use policies as a basic step for generative AI.[^13]
Hold back real past cases the advisor never sees, and test the output on them before you trust it.
Price the lift: hours saved a month times loaded cost per hour (pay plus benefits). Subtract seat costs, upkeep and the hours your checkers spend.
Ask whether any paid mapping work ends in a pilot. One clinic group's ops lead feared paying for a roadmap deck nobody uses.[^32]

faq.q: How much does an AI consultant cost?
faq.a: We found no neutral fee data, so get a fixed price in writing; business AI seats alone run $14 to $21 per person a month.[^26][^27][^23] Cost is also driven by staff time and any systems you connect.

faq.q: What is the 10-20-70 rule for AI?
faq.a: BCG's 10-20-70 rule of thumb says about 10% of AI effort goes to algorithms, 20% to technology and data, and 70% to people and process.[^7] RAND's interviews point the same way: the top failure is a misunderstood problem.[^8]

faq.q: What is the best AI program for a small business?
faq.a: Usually the one built into what you already pay for. Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace both sell AI on business plans of up to 300 users.[^27][^26] Pick on fit with your email and files, not on rankings.

faq.q: When does a custom AI agent make sense, versus ChatGPT or our existing tools?
faq.a: Rarely for a first project at this size. Most small-firm AI use is writing and everyday work that business seats already cover.[^12] Gartner says many jobs sold as agents don't need one.[^33]

faq.q: Should a consultant map our workflows first, or is that wasted money?
faq.a: Map only the job you will pilot, and tie the mapping to that pilot. RAND found a misunderstood problem is the top reason AI projects fail.[^8] One clinic group's ops lead called mapping with no pilot "paid discovery fluff".[^32]

pickElse: Under about 40 staff, or not ready to pay: start with a free Small Business Development Center (SBDC) advisor trained in AI.[^9] America's SBDC says its AI U program has coached 8,000+ businesses.[^9]
You make things: call your state's Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) center first.[^10] Some help fund staff AI training, as Maryland's did for a family apple processor.[^34]
Staff only need help with everyday writing: buy business seats from the table above and train people.[^12][^23]
One clear workflow between two systems: see our AI automation consulting guide, and keep the first project small enough to manage.[^14] A plan across several departments: see AI strategy consulting.

offer.heading: Running a firm of 40 to 150 staff? Pick your first AI job in 30 minutes
offer.body: Free, before any paid work, and no sales pitch: 30 minutes on your first workflow. Bring one job that eats staff time. You leave with the job to start with, who on your staff should own it, and the seats it needs.

reviews.notes: Read as Dana, the COO who builds the shortlist. Got the first job, the before-and-after number and who does what in 10 seconds. Recipe 2 had no decision date, so it now ends with a keep, change or stop call at eight weeks. Wanted a sourced figure for owner hours per week; none exists in the research, so the page asks the advisor instead of inventing one.

Tripped on SBDC, MEP and 'rollout gate'. SBDC and MEP are now spelled out on first use; recipe 3 now says 'a go-or-stop check before rollout'. Every flow step names a role and reads on a phone. The seat table stays five short columns, with seat limits in the plan name.

Asked whether one site can go first and what it costs the unit. Recipe 3 pilots in one team or site; the seat table gives a ten-person pilot cost. The price-the-lift step left out checker time, so it now subtracts the hours people spend checking AI output.

Read as the ops lead who would run the first project. Wanted authority, not just tasks: the human-role bullet now says the ops lead can stop the pilot. The 'no time' watch-out now says who blocks the hours (the owner-CEO). Would like a sourced size for a hold-out test; none in the research, so no number is given.

Steve self-selects in from the title (40-150 staff). He wants a consulting price; the page gives none because every range found was a vendor's own, and answers with seat costs and cost drivers instead. The seat table read as 'buy 150 seats', so the intro now says a pilot needs far fewer. His worries are covered: data (one approved tool), rules (Colorado, as of Nov 2026), skills (training), return (price the lift), paying for slides (the mapping question). Missing: a measured AI case at exactly his size; the nearest public one is about 200 staff.
